learningObjective: Identify sound and unsound assumptions in alias analysis and their effect on downstream optimizations.

canonicalClaims.claim: A sound alias analysis is a may-analysis (over-approximation); may-alias never breaks correctness but may inhibit optimizations. Must-alias is a stronger property enabling optimizations across pointers. False no-alias is a soundness bug because downstream passes trust the analysis and may reorder or eliminate memory operations incorrectly.
conditions: The compiler operates on a standard may/no/must alias framework.
Downstream passes rely on the analysis without re-verifying their aliasing assumptions.
nonImplications: Does not imply must-alias is common; typically only trivial cases yield must-alias.
Does not imply may-alias is useless; it soundly bounds behavior for unknown pointers.

misconceptions.claim: Reporting 'no-alias' when pointers may alias is safe because downstream passes re-verify aliasing.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Downstream passes trust the analysis; unsound no-alias leads to reordered stores/loads and miscompilation.

misconceptions.claim: May-alias is unsound because it prevents legitimate optimizations.
misconceptions.whyWrong: May-alias is sound but imprecise; it foregoes optimizations conservatively rather than risking incorrect ones.

misconceptions.claim: Must-alias and may-alias mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Must-alias is a strict subset of may-alias; must-alias implies aliasing in every execution, may-alias implies aliasing in some execution.

implementationFacts: LLVM provides AliasAnalysis / AAResults interfaces returning MayAlias, MustAlias, PartialAlias, NoAlias.
Steensgaard and Andersen are canonical scalable pointer analyses; may-alias by design.
Type-based alias analysis (TBAA) uses type disjointness to prove no-alias.
performanceScenarios: LICM cannot hoist a load over a store unless alias analysis proves no-alias.
Autovectorization requires the compiler to prove non-aliased array accesses.
